entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Robert I of Burgundy, known as the Old or the Headstrong, was Duke of Burgundy from 1032 to his death in 1076. Born to King Robert II of France and Constance of Arles, Robert was the third son of the French monarch and had a tumultuous relationship with his brother, Henry I of France.

As Duke of Burgundy, Robert expanded the Duchy's borders through strategic alliances and military campaigns. He also oversaw the construction of several castles and fortified towns, including the famous Château du Jouy-en-Touraine.

Robert's legacy as Duke of Burgundy is complex and multifaceted. He played a significant role in the formation of the Holy Roman Empire and was a key figure in the development of the Carolingian Renaissance. Despite his military successes, Robert's personal life was marked by conflict and instability, including a series of bitter feuds with his brother and other nobles.

As a lasting cultural footprint, Robert I of Burgundy's reign saw the emergence of a distinct Burgundian identity, characterized by a unique blend of French, Germanic, and Roman influences. This identity would go on to shape the history of Western Europe for centuries to come.

In the words of the 12th-century historian, William of Newburgh, 'Robertus Burgundio, dux magnus et potens, qui in suo tempore multa et mirabilia fecit' ('Robert of Burgundy, a great and powerful duke, who in his time did many and wonderful things').
